topics.title: 41.1 Asynchronous events
topics.summary: An asynchronous signal can arrive independently of the interrupted statement’s purpose. The program may be halfway through updating a data structure or holding a library’s internal lock. Handler code must not assume a clean application boundary. Synchronous fault signals have a different relationship to execution: they result from an instruction’s behavior. Catching such a signal does not automatically make corrupted state recoverable. Treat routine notifications and invalid-memory faults as different design problems.

topics.title: 41.2 Signal delivery
topics.summary: Signal disposition defines whether a signal is handled, ignored, or given its default action, subject to signals that cannot be caught or ignored. Signal masks control which signals are blocked for a thread. In a multithreaded process, dispositions and per-thread masks have different scopes. Process-directed signals can be delivered to an eligible thread under the platform’s rules. A design that depends on one particular worker receiving a signal should use a deliberate masking and signal-consumption strategy instead of leaving delivery accidental.

topics.title: 41.3 kill
topics.summary: Despite its name, kill sends a signal; the chosen signal’s disposition determines the effect. It can request termination, notify, or test certain existence/permission conditions with signal number zero under documented rules. A PID is a reusable identifier, not an eternal object reference. Long-lived supervisors must account for lifecycle and identity races. This book’s simple examples use freshly created children or the current process rather than treating an old stored PID as permanently trustworthy.

topics.title: 41.4 sigaction
topics.summary: sigaction installs a handler and associated mask and flags. It provides explicit control that is preferable to relying on historically varying signal semantics. Initialize the structure and signal set before installing it. Flags such as SA_RESTART affect some interrupted operations, not every possible wait or system call. Correct I/O code still needs to interpret its own interface’s results. A blanket assumption that signals can never interrupt operations is unsafe.

topics.title: 41.5 Signal handlers
topics.summary: A minimal handler records that an event occurred and leaves substantial work to ordinary control flow. A volatile sig_atomic_t flag supports the limited communication pattern used here. It is not a general atomic counter or a substitute for C++ inter-thread synchronization. Do not call printf , allocate memory, acquire arbitrary mutexes, or use ordinary C++ stream operations from an asynchronous handler. They may rely on state that the interrupted code was modifying. Use only operations guaranteed async-signal-safe for the relevant environment. [ R20 ]

topics.title: 41.6 Blocking signals
topics.summary: Blocking delays delivery; it does not necessarily discard the event. A critical setup sequence can block a signal, install state, and then unblock it at a controlled point. In multithreaded programs, use the appropriate thread-aware mask interfaces and establish masks before creating workers when that is part of the design. Blocking is also needed to close a check-then-sleep race. The signal must not slip between observing a flag and entering a wait that would then have no future notification to wake it.

topics.title: 41.7 Pending signals
topics.summary: A blocked signal can become pending. Standard signals generally do not queue one distinct instance for every repeated occurrence; multiple occurrences can coalesce. A SIGCHLD notification should trigger collection of all available child statuses, not one wait per presumed signal instance.

topics.title: 41.8 Signal safety
topics.summary: Signal safety concerns reentrancy and permitted operations at an asynchronous interruption point. It is not the same as ordinary thread safety. A function protected by an internal mutex can be thread-safe yet deadlock when called from a handler that interrupted a thread holding that mutex. A handler using an async-signal-safe function that can affect errno should save and restore errno when necessary. A self-pipe pattern can notify an event loop with a small write, but it must handle a full nonblocking pipe without blocking inside the handler.

topics.title: 41.9 Signal races
topics.summary: A race occurs when correctness depends on the timing of delivery relative to ordinary state changes. Installing a handler after enabling an event source can miss the intended handling window. Updating shared bookkeeping without a masking plan can expose inconsistent state. Design the state transition and notification together. The signal says that something may have changed; protected ordinary code determines exactly what changed and performs the required work. This parallels condition-variable design in Part XI.

topics.title: 41.10 Sleep/wakeup races
topics.summary: The broken pattern is if (!flag) pause(); : a signal can set the flag after the check but before pause , leaving the program asleep after the only notification. Making the flag volatile does not make those two operations atomic. sigsuspend temporarily installs a signal mask and waits as one coordinated operation. Block the relevant signal while checking the predicate, then use a mask that permits it during the wait. On return, recheck the predicate in a loop. [ R40 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Safe signal notification
topics.summary: A signal handler should do minimal async-signal-safe work. A common pattern sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag or writes a byte to a self-pipe, then returns. Normal code observes the flag or file descriptor and performs complex processing outside the handler. Calling arbitrary allocation or I/O library functions inside the handler can violate reentrancy requirements.

Signal safety concerns reentrancy and permitted operations at an asynchronous interruption point. It is not the same as ordinary thread safety. A function protected by an internal mutex can be thread-safe yet deadlock when called from a handler that interrupted a thread holding that mutex. A handler using an async-signal-safe function that can affect errno should save and restore errno when necessary. A self-pipe pattern can notify an event loop with a small write, but it must handle a full nonblocking pipe without blocking inside the handler.

SLIDE 22: 41.10 Sleep/wakeup races

The broken pattern is if (!flag) pause(); : a signal can set the flag after the check but before pause , leaving the program asleep after the only notification. Making the flag volatile does not make those two operations atomic. sigsuspend temporarily installs a signal mask and waits as one coordinated operation.
